newsitem.title: USA: Key senator urges Weld to drop out of Mexico fight.
newsitem.headline: Key senator urges Weld to drop out of Mexico fight.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said on Thursday fellow Republican William Weld should give up his fight to become ambassador to Mexico and refused to force conservative Sen. Jesse Helms to hold a confirmation hearing.

His sharply worded advice to the former Massachusetts governor: "Accept consideration for another post or look for work," seemed to doom the Weld nomination which has run up against a brick wall in the form of Helms.

In comments to reporters the Mississippi Republican also questioned Weld's diplomatic qualifications. "You have a nominee that has talked in a way that is certainly not diplomatic and acted in a way that you wonder 'is this what we want to be an ambassador?'"

Lott's remarks were made just as Weld was to come to Capitol Hill to seek, as he said, "a fair hearing" in the Senate. Weld was to meet with Helms, a North Carolina Republican, and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry, his rival in the 1996 Senate race.

A White House official said President Bill Clinton would continue to fight for Weld's nomination and played down the significance of Lott's remarks. "I wouldn't read too much into any one comment on any one day," said the White House official who asked not to be identified."

The administration and Senate Democrats insisted that Weld was fully qualified and would be confirmed if the Senate were allowed to vote. Lott announced he would not use his power as Majority Leader to intervene for Weld against Helms.
"I am not going to be a part of a grandstanding and trying to roll the chairman when it is not necessary," he said.
Helms has vowed not to hold a hearing, effectively blocking it from a Senate vote, due to Weld's stance on social issues and his record on fighting drugs.

From the moderate wing of the Republican, Weld surprised many by stepping down earlier this week after 6 1/2 years as governor of Massachusetts to battle against the Helms, arch-conservative, and powerful chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The issue has divided the party and several Republican senators from Northeastern states have vowed to battle alongside the former governor.
"A fair hearing is all I'm looking for," Weld told reporters as he called at the State Department to meet senior officials. "I call on Senator Helms to explain why there shouldn't be a fair hearing."

Helms charges that Weld is "soft" on drugs, and inappropriate for the post in Mexico, a major transit route for narcotics reaching the United States. Weld denies the charge, but Helms cites Weld's support for medicinal use of marijuana.

Lott, without suggesting Weld be nominated for a specific post other than Mexico, noted the administration has vacancies in both Canada and Mexico. But he ended his comments with further questioning of Weld's handling of the nomination: "Diplomats are supposed to stop fights, not create fights."

Weld also attended briefings on Mexico at the State Department. After meeting with several senators, Weld was to return to the State Department to see Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and Under Secretary of State Thomas Pickering.

Despite predictions that his nomination was doomed, Weld told reporters at the State Department: "I don't really have a sense one way or the other. I'm just looking forward to meeting with the State Department folks today and the senators."

Weld, a Spanish-speaker, said his aim was to learn "a little bit more about Mexico than even I've picked up in the last few weeks and talk to some senators, drop a penny in the well, listen for the echo."
